claims.text: The superconducting transition temperature in Ti–Hf–Zr–V–Cr high-entropy alloys is governed primarily by average valence electron concentration.
Valence electron concentration changes the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the electronic density of states at the Fermi level modulate electron–phonon coupling strength.
The baseline Ti–Hf–Zr–V–Cr alloy produced by arc melting and rapid quenching is a homogeneous, single-phase disordered solid solution.
Systematically varying Ti content while keeping every element above 5 at.% adjusts the alloy's overall valence electron concentration.
X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy can be used to check whether secondary phases or ordering emerge during the compositional adjustments.
Changing Ti concentration adjusts the total electron count.
Changing the total electron count influences electron–phonon coupling strength.
Electron–phonon coupling strength affects Cooper-pair formation efficiency.
Changes in Cooper-pair formation efficiency alter the superconducting transition temperature.
The superconducting transition temperature will vary non-monotonically with valence electron concentration.
At least one tested composition will have a superconducting transition temperature that is optimal relative to the baseline.
The transition-temperature trend will exhibit a distinct extremum at an optimal valence electron concentration.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloys remain single-phase, disordered solid solutions without phase separation or long-range ordering.
Minor compositional adjustments may also change local ordering or defect concentrations.
A lack of systematic correlation between valence electron concentration and transition temperature under structurally controlled conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
